newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE-EMU Bank regulation still unresolved issue.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-EMU Bank regulation still unresolved issue.

text.p: The regulation and safeguarding of banks under a common European currency remains an unresolved issue, and some are starting to worry that the powers of a European Central Bank (ECB) may be insufficient.

Unlike the Federal Reserve, which has authority in numerous areas of banking supervision, the ECB will, under its current mandate, play more of an advisory and consultative role in overseeing Europe's banks.
Its diminished authority stems largely from the Maastricht treaty which gives greater weight to national monetary authorities and EU finance ministers.
Under the treaty, EU finance ministers have authority to do the following:

"Acting unanimously on a proposal from the Commission and after consulting the ECB and after receiving the assent of the European Parliament, confer upon the ECB specific tasks concerning policies relating to the prudential supervision of credit institutions and other financial institutions."
SUBSIDIARY COMPLICATIONS

This heavily hedged statement is complicated further by the EU's rules of subsidarity, say analysts. A bank in one country may establish subsidiaries and branches in other EU countries. However, each bank will be subject to home-country supervision.
Some see this arrangement as a potential source of trouble.
"In a system of segmented financial markets, differences in bank regulation can be tolerated. In intergrated markets they cannot," says Peter Kenen, economist at America's Princeton University.
Among the worries analysts have with a banking system that has insufficient centralised control, several stand out.

First, not all bank customers are domestic residents. A financial failure in the home country could be felt by foreign depositors as well. Moreover, the failure of one bank might cast doubt on the ability of other banks in a country to survive.
Related to such concerns are today's integrated financial markets, where a mishap in one country could spread quickly across Europe and possibly into international financial centres.
LENDER OF LAST RESORT
Experts say all of these factors argue for clarification over the role national central banks and the ECB would have as lenders of last resort during a crisis.

Under the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) national central banks will be partners in an arrangement which puts the ECB at the center of monetary policy-making. But regulation will remain largely in the hands of the former.

Dirk Schoenmaker, an economist at the Bank of England, says two important questions need to be answered under this scenario: Will national central banks continue their lender of last resort operations at their own choice and on their own account, and is there a need for the ECB to preserve European-wide systemic stability?
"When responsibility is not clearly allocated, there is a risk that a crisis will be exacerbated by delays in the provision of assistance," says Schoenmaker.
"Such delays may be due to misunderstandings and disputes among potential lenders of last resort about who is responsible," he added.

As an example, Schoenmaker puts forward the hypothetical case of a large French company that issues commerical paper in London which is bought by the London branch of a Portuguese bank. Suppose the French company faces financial problems and cannot repay its debt at maturity.

Possible implications involve uncertainty in the London market and doubts about the solvency of the Portuguese bank. The question then becomes which central bank -- the Bank of England, the Banque de France or the Banco de Portugal -- is responsible to intervene.

Most analysts have concluded that official intervention should depend on the scale of the problem. Support for individual banks can still be given at the local level by national central banks on their own account.
But problems affecting EMU-wide markets will require ECB intervention. The primary worry is what happens when local problems become cross-border headaches.
BANKING SUPERVISION

Here again, the treaty provides greater powers to national authorities. At present, 10 of the 15 national central banks in the EU are directly responsible for banking supervision, with the remaining five having indirect involvement.
Several studies have suggested a variety of approaches toward supervision, with some focusing on the distinction between small and large international banks.

A recent report by the Brussels-based Centre for European Policy Studies argues for a two-tier structure, with national authorities responsible for smaller and medium-sized banks and the ECB in control of big multinationals.

The problem, however, is the limitations the ECB is under. One way around this problem, say experts, is for the ECB to get its information from the EU's Banking Supervisory Sub-Committee, a group which brings together members of national central banks and supervisory authorities.

Alternatively, EU finance ministers could be given greater influence in the oversight of banks, particularly since EMU would likely prompt consolidation in the financial industry -- including banks, securities houses and insurance companies.
